Seat and client churn: exploratory analysis (2026, with 2024–2026 history)¶

Who this is for. Executives read the opening of each section and the charts; the data team opens the collapsible Method, counts and caveats blocks for definitions, denominators and checks.

Where the numbers come from. Every 2026 headline figure is computed from the workbook Churn Analysis 10312026 - updated.xlsx with the workbook's own definitions and is checked against the workbook's Client Raw, Churn Report, Data Checks and view sheets (Section 1, asserted). Trends longer than 2026 use the model labels from notebook 01 (data/processed) and say so in the chart subtitle.

How to run. ./eda/run_eda.sh executes this notebook top to bottom in a fresh kernel with papermill and writes the code-free HTML export. The notebook refuses to run without the fixed environment or on a different input file.

Reading the charts. Patterns are associations, not causes. Every rate shows its n; segment rates carry Wilson 95% intervals; small segments are greyed out; September and October 2026 are marked incomplete because disengagement tickets for those months are still arriving.

Configuration¶

CONFIG is the only place where a threshold, window, band, colour or path is set. Each entry has a value, a source (brief, user, workbook, data-derived or claude-code-proposed) and a one-line why. Functions receive the plain value dict P; they never read notebook state.

Shared functions¶

Loading and cleaning, the chart and table helpers that apply the visual standards, and small statistics helpers. Section-specific functions are defined at the start of each section. Every function is pure: inputs are arguments, outputs are return values; an audit at the end of the notebook checks that no function reads notebook state.

Privacy. Staff names, usernames, free-text ticket comments and ticket submitter fields are dropped as the sheets are loaded. Staff are never identified; client names appear only when show_client_names is True.

Load and prepare the data¶

The workbook is read once. Three working tables are built from it:

  • client-months 2026 (Client Raw as is, plus segment, size band, tenure band, industry group);
  • 2026 exits with workbook labels (Engagement Raw rows with Inscope Churn = yes, using the workbook's own reason, replacement note and ticket columns, joined to the client-month they happened in);
  • client headcount history 2023–2026, rebuilt from Engagement Raw with the workbook's counting rules and asserted to reproduce Client Raw exactly for 2026.

The model labels from notebook 01 are joined to the same exits so the two label versions can be compared.

Loaded in 7s | client-months 9,719 | 2026 exits 1,950 | engagements 31,126 (in-scope base 20,982) | UB4108 tickets 6,799 | model-label exits 5,853

1.2 Glossary¶

Term Plain-English meaning
Seat One staff member placed with a client (one engagement). Headcount = number of seats.
In-scope Seats at real clients. Internal pools (RTG, Hub, Disengaged Staff Pool) and test clients are out of scope.
Opening / closing seats Seats at the start of the month (started before the 1st and not ended before it) / at the end of the month.
Upsell A seat that starts during the month (new client or existing client).
Exit A seat that ends during the month. The workbook files each exit under one reason: Business Reasons, Service Dissatisfaction, Resignation, or Other (paperwork records, retractions, unknown).
Downsell An exit at a client that still has seats at month-end.
Churn (to zero) An exit in the month a client's seats fall to zero. The workbook counts it once per client, in the latest month it reached zero.
Pause A client that reached zero and later had seats again (a returning client).
Replacement The workbook counts an exit as replaced when its ticket says "with Replacement" (stated intent). Notebook 01 also measures observed replacement: a new seat started at the same client in the same month.
Unreplaced exit An exit with a reason (Business, Service, Resignation) that was not replaced. This is what "seat churn" means in this notebook.
Seat churn rate Unreplaced exits per 100 opening seats per month.
Gross churn % All exits ÷ opening seats (the workbook's "Lost % of opening HC").
Net churn % (All exits − upsells) ÷ opening seats (the workbook's formula). Negative means the business grew.
New Logo vs Organic A start or exit within 12 months of the client's very first seat is New Logo; after that it is Organic.
Segment (5+ / under 5) Set every month from the client's opening seats that month.
Client flag Set once for the year from seats on 1 Jan: Base 5+, Base under 5, Grew into 5+, New logo 5+, New logo under 5.
Brand Cloudstaff or Opti (two subsidiaries of one business). VAR clients count as Cloudstaff, as in the workbook.
Pull-out A client losing at least 5 seats and at least 30% of its opening seats (unreplaced) in one month.
Workbook labels / model labels Workbook labels follow the workbook's rules (2026 only, used for every headline number). Model labels are notebook 01's corrected labels (May 2024 – Oct 2026), used only for longer trends.
Wilson interval The range the true rate plausibly lies in (95%), given how many seats it is based on.

1.4 Two label versions: where they differ for 2026¶

Headline numbers use the workbook labels. The model labels (notebook 01) correct how tickets are matched to exits, measure replacement by observed hires and date exits by the notice date. This bridge shows the size of each difference on the same 2026 exits.

What this shows. Of the 1,950 exits in 2026, 146 are matched to a different disengagement ticket by the model labels than by the workbook, and 27 change reason. Unreplaced exits are 1,108 with workbook labels and 1,237 with model labels.

So what. The workbook's reason split is reliable at the total level but not for every exit; the main driver is that the workbook takes the first ticket ever filed for a person at a client, which for re-hired or long-serving staff can be an old, cancelled request. Headline numbers stay on the workbook definitions so they match the reports executives already see.

Caveats. The brief expected about 385 mislabelled exits; that figure covers the whole May 2024 – Oct 2026 window in notebook 01 (390 changed exits). The count here is for 2026 only.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Ticket comparison: workbook Uber Ticket vs the UB4108 row the model chose (ub_idx, latest non-cancelled ticket submitted 180 days before to 60 days after the exit). Model tickets belong to the same client in 99.4% of cases (asserted > 99%).

2. Headcount overview¶

In short. Seats grew from 5,826 on 1 January to 6,325 on 31 October 2026 (+8.6%): 2,449 new seats more than offset 1,950 exits. Exits ran at about 195 a month all year; growth came from upsells, not from lower exits.

So what. Growth in 2026 came from adding seats, not from losing fewer: exits were steady at 176–208 a month. Opti's net growth is +36 seats on a base of 855.

Caveats. September and October exit counts are final in headcount, but their reasons may still change as late tickets are logged. Upsells include brand-new clients; Section 9 splits New Logo from Organic growth.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Exits = Downsell + Churn for each reason, plus Other exits (For Record Purpose Only, Retraction, no reason). Totals match the Churn Report and Data Checks (Section 1.3).

So what. Year to date, net churn is -8.6% of the 1 January base (the Churn Report's YTD formula), i.e. seats grew. Gross churn is flat month to month, so the month-to-month swings in net churn come from upsells (e.g. March).

Caveats. Opti's rates move more because its base is about a tenth of Cloudstaff's. The workbook has no growth % formula; growth % here is upsells ÷ opening seats (listed as a proposed setting for review).

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

YTD net churn % = YTD (exits − upsells) ÷ January opening HC, exactly as the Churn Report's YTD column.

What this shows. A longer, 30-month view of seat churn that 2026 alone cannot give, using notebook 01's corrected labels.

So what. The monthly rate in Jan–Aug 2026 (2.16%) is close to Jan–Oct 2025 (2.33%): 2026 is not an unusual year. Large one-off events, not a rising trend, drive the peaks.

Caveats. Model labels date an exit by the notice date (often weeks before the last day) and count observed replacement, so monthly counts do not match the workbook's 2026 columns (bridge in Section 1.4). Notebook 01 treats only months up to Jul 2026 as complete; Aug is ~90% complete, Sep–Oct well below.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Seats at risk = rows of seat_month_panel per month (active in-scope seats at the start of the month whose exit has not yet been notified). Unreplaced = y_1m.

3. Who churns: seat churn rates by segment¶

Seat churn rate = unreplaced exits ÷ opening seats, per month, shown per 100 seats. Workbook labels, Jan–Oct 2026. Each segment is defined by the client-month the exit happened in (the same row of Client Raw), so numerator and denominator always describe the same clients and months.

In short. On average 1.84 of every 100 seats leave unreplaced each month (workbook labels; 1,105 unreplaced exits over 60,133 seat-months). The rate is highest at 1-seat clients (3.75) and lowest at 6-15-seat clients (1.62); small clients lose a larger share of their seats, large clients lose more seats in total.

What this shows. How fast seats are lost, unreplaced, for each brand, client segment and client age (New Logo = first 12 months).

So what. Under-5 clients' rate is clearly higher than the 5+ rate; Opti's is clearly lower than Cloudstaff's. New-logo clients' rate is not clearly different from established (Organic) clients'. Associations only: small or new clients differ from large ones in many ways at once.

Caveats. Unreplaced uses the ticket's stated intent ('with Replacement'), the only replacement field the workbook has. Section 8 shows how often a replacement actually started. New Logo here is the client's first 12 months at the start of the month; the workbook tags each exit by its own date, so a few exits near the 12-month mark fall on the other side.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

3 unreplaced exits happened at clients with no opening seats that month (joined and left in the same month) and have no denominator; they are left out of segment rates but are in every count. Segment = 5+ if opening HC ≥ 5 that month (Churn Report rule).

What this shows. Which reasons drive churn in each client size band.

So what. Business-reason exits (a client cutting roles or budget) fall steadily with client size, from 2.36 to 0.56. Service-dissatisfaction exits do the opposite: at 51+ clients they are the largest reason (0.68). For small clients the lever is the client's business; for large clients it is service quality. Resignations vary little with size (except 1-seat clients).

Caveats. Cells with few exits are noisy: read the n. Small-client Service Dissatisfaction is partly reclassified to Business Reasons by the rehire rule (Section 4.5).

Same denominator as Figure 03_02, split by reason.

4. Why: exit reasons¶

All counts are 2026 exits with workbook labels (Engagement Raw FINAL REASON FOR DISENGAGEMENT, which is what Client Raw counts). Other = For Record Purpose Only, Retraction and exits with no reason.

In short. Business reasons (the client cutting roles or budget) are the largest single cause: 734 of 1,950 exits (38%), followed by resignations (32%) and service dissatisfaction (22%). About 60% of exits are decided by the client or by Cloudstaff, not the staff member. The mix is stable month to month.

5. Clients: contraction, churn and concentration¶

In short. 191 clients went to zero seats in 2026 (workbook count), almost all with fewer than 5 seats; about 7% of clients that reach zero start a seat again within a year. Seat exposure is concentrated: the 20 largest clients hold 36% of seats.

What this shows. How many clients lost all their seats each month, and how many later came back.

So what. Going to zero is a small-client event (1 of the 2026 cases had 5+ opening seats that month). Returns are uncommon (7% within a year) and, when they happen, usually quick (median gap 2 months), which suggests pauses between roles rather than won-back clients.

Caveats. Only 8 of the 2026 zero clients had seats again by 31 Oct (Data Checks: 8). Recent zero events have had little time to return; the Kaplan–Meier curve accounts for that. 'Coming back' counts any new seat, even a single one.

Zero events 2023–Oct 2026: 836 (of which 192 in 2026; the workbook's 191 counts each client once). Returned: 57; gap months median 2, quartiles 1–4.

What this shows. What a pull-out looks like up close: the largest event in the history.

So what. The client went from 225 seats at its peak to 6 today. The client gave notice in November 2024 (notice dates 06 Nov–27 Nov; median 41 days before the last day), but most tickets were filed only weeks later (median 3 days before the last day). The warning existed early; the ticket system recorded it late. An alert when several notices arrive at one client would have given the account team about a month more to respond.

Caveats. Anonymised by default. Model labels date these exits to the notice month (November 2024), which is why the long-term chart (02_04) peaks then; by last day, the losses are spread over December to February. The brief's context figures (119 of 140 seats, tickets 6 Dec – 1 Jan) differ slightly from these; see the review pack.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Client chosen as the largest pull-out with a notice month in Nov–Dec 2024 (CONFIG pullout_case_month).

6. When: seat tenure and survival¶

Survival curves need exits over several years, so this section uses the model labels (reason-coded exits from April 2024). Seats are followed from April 2024 (or their start, if later) to their exit or to 31 Oct 2026. A seat that started before April 2024 enters the analysis at the tenure it had then (left truncation), so long-serving seats are counted correctly. An event is a real departure (Business, Service or Resignation, replaced or not); paperwork records, retractions, internal moves and exits with no ticket are treated as censored.

In short. About 39% of new seats end within their first year and 57% within two (model labels). Risk is highest early: in the first 3 months a seat ends at 4.6 per 100 a month, against 2.6 after the first year.

7. Warning time: tickets and notice¶

How much notice the business gets before a seat's last day. Workbook labels: each 2026 exit's ticket is the one the workbook matched (Uber Ticket). Because that match is sometimes an old ticket (Section 11.4), the same measures with the model's corrected ticket are shown in the detail block.

In short. Today the business gets a median of 23 days' warning before a seat's last day (earliest of ticket or notice date). 28% of tickets are filed after the person has already left, and 30% of notice dates equal the last day, so for a large share of exits the systems give no usable warning at all.

Table 07_01. Warning time by reason
reason exits with ticket median days ticket→last day median days TND→last day share ticket filed after last day share TND = last day median warning (days) median warning, model ticket (days)
Business Reasons 728 25.0 30.0 22.1% 25.5% 30.0 30.0
Service Dissatisfaction 431 0.0 0.0 48.5% 51.7% 0.0 0.0
Resignation 623 21.0 28.0 22.5% 22.6% 28.0 28.0
Other 112 84.0 85.0 17.9% 17.0% 85.0 2.0

What this shows. How far ahead of the last day the ticket and the notice date are.

So what. Service Dissatisfaction exits are usually recorded on or after the last day (48% of tickets filed after the person left): these are often immediate removals, so the business learns about them when they have already happened. Business Reasons and Resignation exits give a few weeks' notice.

Caveats. Days are calendar days. Long negative tails (tickets filed weeks after the exit) are paperwork catching up, not warning.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Tickets: 1,894 of 1,950 exits have a workbook-matched UB4108 ticket. With the model's corrected ticket match the median warning is 22 days (workbook match: 23).

What this shows. How much time there is to act before a seat is lost.

So what. Half of exits give 23 days or less. An early-warning model (notebook 01) is only useful if it flags risk before a ticket exists; for most client-driven exits, the ticket itself arrives too late for retention.

Caveats. A notice date equal to the last day is probably a default value, not real notice (Section 11.5), so true notice may be longer than recorded.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Warning = last day − earliest of (ticket submission day, Termination Notice Date when it falls between the start and the last day), floored at 0.

8. Replacement¶

The workbook records only the ticket's stated intent ("with Replacement"). Whether a replacement actually started is measured with notebook 01's observed replacement (model labels, decision D1): a new seat started at the same client in the same calendar month, matched one-to-one in date order, re-papered restarts excluded. Exits are the 2026 exits that carry a reason under the model labels.

In short. About 32% of exits are replaced in the same month by a new seat at the same client (observed), and 33% within 30 days. Exits where the client still needs the role (service dissatisfaction, resignation) are backfilled far more often than business-reason exits. The ticket's stated intent and what actually happened agree on 70% of exits.

What this shows. How often a lost seat is filled again by a new person at the same client.

So what. When the client still needs the role (the person was not working out, or resigned) the seat is often backfilled; when the client cuts the role (business reasons) it mostly is not. Unreplaced business-reason exits are therefore real lost seats, while many service and resignation exits are a recruiting cost rather than lost revenue. Small clients and Opti backfill much less often.

Caveats. Observed replacement counts any new seat at the client, which may be a different role. One-to-one matching keeps a single hire from replacing two exits.

9. Upsell and growth¶

Workbook definitions, Jan–Oct 2026: an upsell is any seat that starts in the month; New Logo upsells are at clients within 12 months of their first seat, Organic at established clients (Client Raw Upsell: New Logo / Organic).

In short. Of 2,449 new seats in 2026, 1,390 (57%) came from established clients and 1,059 from new logos. Clients already with us on 1 January ended October with 98% of their January seats (seat-weighted net retention), so the existing base shrank on its own.

11.4 The first-match ticket problem¶

The workbook links each exit to a disengagement ticket with an XLOOKUP on shortcode + username, which returns the first ticket ever filed for that person at that client. For staff with more than one ticket (re-hires, cancelled requests, long tenure) this can be the wrong ticket, with the wrong reason, replacement intent and dates.

What this shows. 146 of the 1,950 exits in 2026 point to a different ticket in the workbook than the one filed for this exit; 27 of them change reason.

So what. Fixing the lookup (take the latest non-cancelled ticket submitted within the months before the exit, as notebook 01 does) would correct reasons, replacement intent and warning-time figures. It is a one-formula change for the workbook owner.

Caveats. The examples are chosen for the largest gap and are therefore the clearest cases, not typical ones.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Model match = notebook 01 decision D3a (latest non-cancelled ticket from 180 days before to 60 days after the exit).

Table 11_06. Notice date equal to the last day, by reason
reason4 tickets equal share
Business Reasons 728 186 25.5%
Service Dissatisfaction 431 223 51.7%
Resignation 623 141 22.6%
Other 112 19 17.0%

What this shows. How often the recorded notice date is simply the last day.

So what. For immediate removals the two can genuinely coincide, but the share is high across all reasons, which points to a defaulted field. If the notice date were recorded reliably it would be the best early-warning date the business has.

Caveats. Exits with no notice date are left out of the denominator.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Equality is on the calendar date.

11.6 September and October are incomplete¶

Tickets and exits keep arriving after the month ends. Using how late exits were recorded in 2025, this compares the expected completeness of each 2026 month with what has been observed so far (model labels, by notice month).

Table 11_07. Expected vs observed label coverage, 2026
month expected_completeness labelled_exits_observed observed_vs_jan_jun_avg

What this shows. Why the last two months look better than they are.

So what. Any chart that ends in September or October understates exits for those months. Executive comparisons should stop at August or say so.

Caveats. By last day (the workbook's view), exits are recorded promptly; it is the reasons and the notice-month view that fill in late.

Method, counts and caveats (data team)

Expected completeness = share of 2025 labelled exits whose last day came within the days left between the month's end and 31 Oct 2026.
